280 curated images. Delivered in 48 hours.

In the first 7 days, the client used 43.

Where they went:
- Press kit
- Social posts
- Internal announcement deck
- Investor update

One day of coverage can turn into months of usable content, if the delivery is curated and fast.

What is the fastest turnaround you have received after an event?

https://whitepaper.site

Most corporate event photos never get used.
Not because they are bad, but because no one planned where they would go.

A common pattern:
- 300 to 500 images land in a shared folder
- the events team moves to the next project
- no one owns distribution
- two weeks later, the press window is gone

In my experience, the fix is rarely "a better photographer".
It is a distribution plan built before the brief is finalized.

What is the biggest bottleneck in your post-event content workflow?

https://whitepaper.site

412 edited images. A 400-person event. Delivered at hour 44.

The hard part was not speed.
It was selection.

A full-day event can generate 1,400 to 1,800 captures. A 48-hour window does not allow slow curation.

A practical selection system:
- Pass 1 (in-field): remove technical failures
- Pass 2 (post-event): cut to candidates by segment
- Pass 3 (final): one definitive image per moment, no near-misses, no duplicates

The outcome is a gallery the client can use immediately, with no extra editing.

What is the longest you have waited for post-event images, and what did it cost you in distribution?

https://whitepaper.site

Fast delivery is not just convenience. It is a strategic advantage.

Many distribution windows are short:
- press releases: 24 to 48 hours after an event
- internal newsletters: best while the atmosphere is fresh
- investor decks: visuals needed before the next meeting

A photographer who delivers within 48 hours keeps those windows open.
A photographer who delivers in a week closes most of them.
